title: Pattern Strip
context: Grade 4, the first working topic of the patterns chapter, and the place where the chapter's whole idea is first made to do some work. An adult sees shapes being copied into blanks. What is actually being settled is that a pattern is a start and a rule, and that the rule is found by looking for what stays the same from one step to the next: a group that repeats, a turn of the same size, one side fewer. Every row of the recap's matching question alternates two shapes, so a child can fill each blank by copying the cell two places back without ever finding a group, and that habit fails on the first pattern with a group of three.

writeup.why: Find the group that repeats, or the move made at every step, and carry a picture pattern on until it comes round to the start again.
writeup.look: A long strip of cells with the last few empty, a turn dial under it, and a ring of numbered places at one side of the stage.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only. 'Pattern Strip' sits in ink at the far left, with a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it. The phase title sits beside the dot on the same line, then the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart stand as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the places filled against the places this phase leaves empty, two numbers in ink. The first climbs by one as each cell or each place on the order line fills, and the second is fixed at what this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The strip runs across the top of the working area: ten cells, each 100 by 100 with 8 between, at 64,222, reaching 1136. Each cell holds one shape, one arrow, or one dot on a plus-shaped outline, drawn at one size and never overlapping its neighbour. The bracket rides a rail under the strip, 1072 by 24 at 64,330, and is dragged to cover any run of cells. Copy light then lights every copy of that run along the whole strip at once, each matching copy underlined in green. A copy that does not match is left unlit, never hidden, and the one cell in it that breaks the match is ringed in reddish purple. The side count row runs under the rail, 1072 by 36 at 64,362, writing each shape's number of straight sides under its cell. The lower band, from 414 to 720, holds the dial on the first three phases. The dial is 160 across and docks under whichever empty cell is being filled, kept inside the working area's right edge, with the turn ring 72 across at its left. Each tap turns the dial's arrow one quarter turn clockwise, the way a clock's hands go, and draws that turn as a vermilion arc. The turn ring fills one quarter at a time and closes at four, when the arrow is home. On the fourth phase the dial is parked and the lower band holds the ring bay instead. The ring is 280 across at 64,420, with up to eight numbered places evenly round it. With two rings on, a second ring of the same size stands at 364,420 and reads the same draw. The draw drum is 120 by 120 at 664,420, and the order line is 440 by 80 at 664,620. The order line fills place by place as the order is read off the ring, and a vermilion arc joins the last number back to the first. Down the right of the canvas the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92), which holds what the child has given. That rectangle is the same on every phase and is never animated in or out. Under it is the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is a shape tray of the cells this strip uses and a turn pad of four arrows, pointing up, right, down and left. Twelve number keys three across take over wherever a count or an order is asked for. A word pad carries this strip's own words: group, repeat, quarter turn, clockwise, sides, first and last. The footer runs 758 to 900. The voice caption sits at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling. The phase bar sits at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, taken from its pictures. Whatever the stage hands over is deep blue: a given term, a bead, the bottom row of a tower, a plain letter, a tile already laid. The first member of a repeating group is deep blue too, and the second member, or a second kind set beside the first, is amber. The step itself is vermilion in every tool without exception: a jump arc and its label, a quarter turn, an operation sign, a key's shift. Whatever the rule makes is green: a next term, a built box, a coded or decoded letter, a copy just laid, a tick. Whatever the child is asked to notice is reddish purple: a broken box, a closed-in gap, a doubled part, a leftover counter, a line put back. The dots of dotted paper are grey and nothing else is. Every bracket, outline, rule and blank is near-black chrome. Chrome never borrows a content colour, and no content colour is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a thing is told by its label or its place before it is told by its colour. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box, never a faded copy of its answer. An order is never drawn as a line with two ends until it has been read off the ring. A line with ends is exactly the picture that stops at the last number, so the ring comes first and the line is only ever a copy of a walk round it.
writeup.finish: The card shows the strip the child finished, its repeating group bracketed and every copy lit, and the ring with the order they read off it.

phases.win: every copy of the group lights along the strip and the blanks fill with the matching shapes
phases.does: draws a bracket over the group they think repeats, watches its copies light, then fills the blanks
phases.goal: the smallest group that repeats fills every blank in a row
phases.says: Which shapes come round again? Put a bracket over them.
phases.check: Away from the screen: make a row of three kinds of thing on your desk. Ask a friend to find the group.
phases.feels: the row is one group laid down again and again, and a blank is only the next place in the group
phases.hands: Before the tool is opened, make a row on a desk with real things: square, square, circle, square, square, circle, in paper cut-outs, caps or beads. Ask for the smallest group that repeats, not for the next thing. Every row of the recap's matching question takes turns between two shapes, so give a group of three early, where copying two places back goes wrong. Let the class find where it breaks, and then ask how a group could be checked without filling any blank at all.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which cells come round again? Second rung, the phase's: does every copy of your group match? Third rung: the strip is cut to two whole copies of the group and one blank, and the child brackets again. The shape tray stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: every row of the recap's matching question takes turns between two shapes, so copying two places back has been right four times running.
wrong.move: copies the cell two places back into every blank, which works while two shapes take turns and finds no group at all.
wrong.screen: the child's shapes stay in the blanks, and a bracket is drawn over the two cells they were copied from. Copy light runs that pair along the strip. On a group of three the copies stop matching at the third cell, which is left unlit and ringed in reddish purple. A bracket over three cells is then offered beside it, and every copy of that one lights.

wrong.why: a longer bracket seems safer, because it holds more of the row inside it.
wrong.move: brackets a run one cell too long, taking in the start of the next copy, and fills the blank from it.
wrong.screen: copy light runs the long bracket along the strip, and each copy drifts one cell further until one does not match. That copy is left unlit with its breaking cell ringed. The child's bracket stays drawn, and it is then shortened one cell at a time, with the copies lit again after each.

phases.screen: a strip of shapes with its last two cells empty and the bracket waiting
phases.soWhat: Find the smallest group that repeats, and every blank takes the cell one whole group before it.

phases.win: the arrow settles and the turn ring closes when four quarter turns bring it home
phases.does: turns the dial until the new arrow repeats the move between the cells before it
phases.goal: the same quarter turn is made at every step, and four of them make a full turn
phases.says: How far did it turn each time? Make the same turn again.
phases.check: Point an arrow up and turn it a quarter turn clockwise three times. Which way does it point now?
phases.feels: the same small turn every time, and after four of them the arrow is back where it began
phases.hands: Give each pair a paper arrow and lay it flat on the desk pointing left. Turn it a quarter turn the way a clock's hands go, and say the new direction aloud. Keep turning and counting until the arrow comes home. Then ask how many turns brought it home, and which way it will point after eight turns, before anyone turns it.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how far did the arrow turn between the last two cells? Second rung, the phase's: which way do a clock's hands go? Third rung: the row is cut to two arrows one quarter turn apart, and the child makes the same turn once. The turn pad stays open.

wrong.why: a quarter turn is the same size either way, and the row shows only where the arrow pointed, not which way it moved between cells.
wrong.move: turns the arrow against a clock's hands, so a row that went up, right, down is carried on the other way round.
wrong.screen: the dial replays the move between the last two cells one quarter at a time, drawing it as a vermilion arc the way a clock's hands go. The child's arrow stays in its cell with its own arc drawn beside it, running the other way. The two arcs stand together, and nothing is marked.

wrong.why: a half turn is the easiest turn to see, because the arrow ends up pointing straight back the way it came.
wrong.move: makes a half turn at every step, so up is followed by down and the arrow never points right or left.
wrong.screen: the turn ring shows the child's move as two quarters filled, where the row made one. The dial then turns from the last cell one quarter at a time, and the arrow lands on a direction the child's row skipped. The child's arrow and the dial's stand side by side.

phases.screen: a row of arrows, each pointing a different way, with the dial under the first empty cell
phases.soWhat: A turning pattern makes the same quarter turn at every step, and four quarter turns make a full turn.
phases.concept: A quarter turn at every step

phases.win: the next shape lands and its count starts the row of numbers again from the top
phases.does: reads the side counts, then chooses the shape for the empty cell
phases.goal: a row can lose one side at each step and then start again from its first shape
phases.says: Count the sides of each one. What happens after three?
phases.check: A row starts with a shape of five sides and loses one each step. Name the shapes until it starts again.
phases.feels: the counts go down one at a time until they cannot go any lower, and then the row starts over
phases.hands: Draw a hexagon, a pentagon, a square and a triangle on the board, and count the sides of each aloud with the class. Ask what shape would have two sides, and let someone try to draw one that closes. Then ask where the row must go after the triangle. Write the side counts under the shapes, so the class sees a list of numbers that starts again.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many sides has the last shape? Second rung, the phase's: can a closed shape with straight sides have fewer than three? Third rung: the row is cut to a square, a triangle and one empty cell, with the row's first shape shown at the left. The shape tray stays open.

wrong.why: the row has lost one side at every step so far, and nothing on the strip says the losing has to stop.
wrong.move: looks for a shape with two sides after the triangle, and draws two straight lines meeting at a point.
wrong.screen: the child's two lines are drawn in the empty cell as they were made. The side counter writes two under them and rings the open end in reddish purple, where no side closes the shape. The strip then shows the row's first shape again after the triangle, and the counts under it start again from the top.

wrong.why: every step so far has been one side fewer, so a jump back up to the first count looks like the rule being broken.
wrong.move: reads the first shape coming back after the triangle as a slip in the row, and carries on losing sides.
wrong.screen: the bracket is drawn over the run from the first shape to the triangle, and copy light lights the second copy, starting at the shape that came back. The side counts under the row are drawn as two runs, the second starting under that shape. The child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a row of shapes with their side counts written under them and one cell empty
phases.soWhat: A row can lose one side at each step until the triangle, and then it starts again from its first shape.
phases.concept: One side fewer, then start again

phases.win: the line fills round the ring and an arc joins the last number back to the first
phases.does: draws the starting number, then reads the order off the ring into the line
phases.goal: an order that goes round comes back to the first number after the last
phases.says: Who goes first? Now go round. Who comes after the last one?
phases.check: Away from the screen: four friends take turns in number order, and three is drawn. Say the whole order.
phases.feels: the order has a start and no end, and the draw decides where the start is
phases.hands: Seat four children in a circle holding number cards one to four, and draw a card from a bag. That number goes first, and the group says the whole order aloud going round. Draw again for a new event and say the order again. Then seat a second group of four beside the first and ask whether it needs a draw of its own. Name nobody; call each child by their number.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which number was drawn? Second rung, the phase's: who comes after the last number? Third rung: the ring is cut to three places with the draw already made, and the child reads it round once. The number keys stay open.

wrong.why: a list of numbers has always stopped at its biggest number, and nothing on a written line says it carries on.
wrong.move: stops the order at the last number, leaving out every player whose number comes before the one drawn.
wrong.screen: the order line keeps the child's numbers and draws the places still to fill as empty outlined boxes. The ring is then walked from the drawn place, each number lighting as it is passed. The walk goes past the last number and on round to the first, and the arc joining them is drawn in vermilion.

wrong.why: the drawn number has to go first, and counting order is the only other order the class has ever used.
wrong.move: writes the drawn number first and then the rest in counting order from one, so a draw of four out of five gives four, one, two, three, five.
wrong.screen: the ring is walked from the drawn place, and each player's neighbour on the ring is lit beside them. The child's line stands under the order the ring gives. The one place where a neighbour changed, four and then one, is ringed in reddish purple.

wrong.why: each team has its own column to fill, and a new column looks as though it needs a new draw.
wrong.move: makes a new draw for the second team, so the two teams start from different numbers in one event.
wrong.screen: two rings stand side by side and read one draw together, and both order lines fill from the same start. The child's second order stays beside its ring, and the drum shows the single number drawn for the event.

phases.screen: numbered places round a ring, with the draw waiting and an empty order line beside it
phases.soWhat: In an order that goes round, whoever is drawn goes first, and after the last number comes the first again.
phases.concept: After the last comes the first

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, when the last place of the order line fills. The line lifts off and bends itself round into a ring, and its two ends meet, so the last number sits beside the first. The drawn start carries a small flag. Drag the flag to any other number and the ring unrolls into a new line from there, with every neighbour kept. It runs as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked either way, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a strip of shapes stands with its last two cells empty and the bracket parked at its left hand end. On the second a row of arrows stands, each pointing a different way, with the dial docked under the first empty cell and its turn ring open. On the third a row of shapes stands with its side counts already written under it and one cell empty. On the fourth the ring bay is open with its numbered places drawn round it, the draw waiting and the order line empty. The running count at the top left holds the places filled against the places this phase leaves empty, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the parked bracket, or the dial, or the empty cell, or the draw, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what comes round again. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any strip of shapes, arrows or dots, any row of shapes, and any ring of up to eight numbered places, with the bracket, the dial, the side counter and the draw all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the group that repeats, a quarter turn at every step, a row that loses a side and starts again, and an order that goes round from a drawn start.
voiceLines: A strip of shapes, and some cells still empty. Find what comes round again.
Which shapes come round again? Put a bracket over them.
How far did it turn each time? Make the same turn again.
Count the sides of each one. What happens after three?
Who goes first? Now go round. Who comes after the last one?
Another row. Find the rule before you fill anything.
Free play. Any strip, any ring, with the bracket, the dial and the draw open.
Look again at what stays the same from one cell to the next.
Every row carried on, and every order brought round to its start.

observations.why: A group one cell too long or too short does not start again at the same place each time, so its copies drift.
observations.soWhat: The group that repeats is found by testing it along the whole row, not by looking at the last two cells.
observations.observe: The copies lit all along the strip only when the bracket covered the smallest group that repeats.

observations.why: Each quarter turn points the arrow a new way, and there are only four ways for it to point.
observations.soWhat: A turning pattern repeats every four steps, so a far step is found by counting in fours.
observations.observe: Four quarter turns closed the ring and brought the arrow back to where it began.

observations.why: A closed shape with straight sides needs at least three, so the row cannot lose another side.
observations.soWhat: Starting again is part of the pattern, so the group runs from the first shape to the triangle.
observations.observe: The side counts went down to three and then went back to the first count.

observations.why: Each player keeps the same neighbour wherever the order starts, so the order has a start but no end.
observations.soWhat: After the last number comes the first, and one draw sets the start for both teams.
observations.observe: The order line bent round into a ring, and the last number sat beside the first.

source_tool.blurb: Find the group that repeats, or the move made at every step, and carry a picture pattern on until it comes round again.

serves.exercise: matching each row of shapes to the shape that completes it
completing the three picture series of a turning arrow, a moving dot and shapes that lose a side
writing the performance order of both teams for the three events still to be filled

source_tool.description: A long strip of cells runs across the stage, each cell holding a shape, an arrow, or a dot on a plus-shaped outline, with the last few cells empty. A bracket control lets the child draw a bracket over the cells they think repeat, and the strip then lights every copy of that group along its whole length, so a group that is too long or too short shows at once as a copy that does not match. A turn dial sits under any empty cell in a row of arrows or dots and turns its arrow one quarter turn clockwise at a time, counting the turns in a small ring beside it that closes at four, so the move between two cells is found by making it rather than by guessing. A side counter writes under each shape how many straight sides it has, so a row that loses a side at every step can be seen doing it, and can be seen to start again once it reaches three. A ring bay lays a numbered order round a circle rather than along a line: players stand on the ring in the order of their numbers, a draw sets which one goes first, and the order is read off the ring from there, round past the last number and back to the first. One draw can be set for two rings at once, so two teams are read off the same start, which the printed closing task implies and never says.
source_tool.art_direction: A strip of cells beside a ring / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a strip of picture cells, a paper arrow on a dial, stepping stones with jump arcs between them, counters that pair up, a tower of boxes each resting on two below, two rings of letters that turn, a ruled board of sums with a slate beside it, and a bench of dotted paper with a tray of tiles.
A repeating group is always shown whole. When a bracket is drawn over it, every copy of it along the row is lit at once, and a copy that does not match is left unlit rather than hidden.

Every step in a series is drawn as an arc from one term to the next with its label on the arc, never as a bare number between two terms, so the step between every pair of neighbours can be read, not only the first.
A counting-down track has a zero stone at its left end and nothing beyond it. No track, board or list is ever drawn running on past zero.

Every box of a number tower rests visibly on exactly two boxes below it, and the operation sign is drawn between each pair of neighbours in every row, so a tower that keeps to one operation shows the same sign all the way up.
The alphabet is always drawn round a circle, twenty-six letters evenly spaced, so the last letter sits beside the first and no letter ever falls off an end.
A line put back into a board is drawn sliding into its place between its neighbours, and the jump labels either side of it are rewritten where they stand, never cleared.

Tiles are drawn at true relative size, edge to edge where they touch, never overlapping unless the frame is showing an overlap on purpose, and a circle is never squeezed to close a gap. A tile drawn taller than it is wide is never called a square.
A shape, a term or a box is told apart by its label or its position first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a shape, a term, a box, a letter or a tile the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. Whatever the stage hands over, a printed term, a bead, the bottom row of a tower, a plain letter of a message and a tile already laid, is deep blue, and so is the first member of a repeating group. The second member of a repeating group, and a second kind set beside the first, is amber. The step itself, a jump arc and its label, a quarter turn, the operation sign between two boxes and the shift a key makes from a letter to its partner, is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter whose whole subject is the rule cannot afford a frame where the step has to be hunted for. Whatever the rule makes, a next term, a box built from the two below it, a coded or decoded letter, a tile carried on and a tick on the can do list, is green. Whatever the child is asked to notice, a box that breaks the tower's operation, a space with tiles closed round it, a part where two tiles lie on top of each other, a counter left without a partner and a missing line put back on a board, is reddish purple. The dots of dotted paper are grey and nothing else is. Every bracket, outline, rule and blank is near-black chrome, and the outer edge of a tiled patch is traced in that plain line and never filled, because it is where the tiling stops and not a gap. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box and never a faded copy of its answer. All of that holds in greyscale, because a jump label sits on its own arc, a broken box keeps its light on after the check has moved past it, a closed-in gap is filled while the outer edge is only outlined, and a leftover counter stands apart from the pairs.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look again at what stays the same from one cell to the next.
voice.onNext: Another row. Find the rule before you fill anything.
voice.opening: A strip of shapes, and some cells still empty. Find what comes round again.
voice.onFinish: Every row carried on, and every order brought round to its start.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any strip, any ring, with the bracket, the dial and the draw open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: A quarter turn at every step
One side fewer, then start again
After the last comes the first

placement.where: After a repeating row has been made with real beads or caps on a desk, and before any blank is filled on paper. The tool is what lights every copy of a chosen group along the strip at once, so a group that does not repeat is seen not to, which a pencil cannot show.

answer_key.rule: A pattern is continued by finding its rule and using it at every step. In a repeating pattern the rule is the smallest group that repeats, and each blank takes the cell one whole group before it. In a turning pattern the rule is the move made at every step; a quarter turn clockwise each time brings the shape back to where it began after four turns. In a row that loses one side at each step, the shapes go down to three sides and then start again, because a closed shape with straight sides needs at least three. In an order that goes round, whoever is drawn goes first and the rest follow in the order of their numbers, and after the last number comes the first again. When one draw sets the start for two teams, both are read from the same number.
answer_key.wrong: The strip lights every copy of the group the child chose, so a copy that does not match stands out, and the move between two cells is made again on the dial one quarter turn at a time with the turns counted aloud. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Look for the smallest group that comes round again: red, blue, blue.
The string has shown that group twice, so the next bead starts the group again with red.
The bead after that is the second bead of the group, which is blue.
items.question: A bead string goes red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, and then two empty places. Which beads go in the two places?
items.checkpoint: Find the smallest group that repeats, and every blank is filled from it.
items.misconception: Copying the last bead, which gives blue for the first place, because no group was found.

steps: A quarter turn clockwise moves the arrow the way a clock's hands go.
From left, one quarter turn points it up, a second points it right and a third points it down.
A fourth quarter turn brings it back to left, because four quarter turns make a full turn.
items.answer: Up, then right, then down, then left again
items.question: An arrow points left. At every step it makes a quarter turn clockwise. Which way does it point after one, two, three and four steps?
items.checkpoint: Every step is the same turn, and four quarter turns bring a shape back to where it began.
items.misconception: Turning the arrow the other way round, or by half a turn, and so skipping a direction.

steps: Count the sides: five, four, three, so each shape has one side fewer than the one before.
After the triangle the row began again with the pentagon, so the group is pentagon, square, triangle.
The empty place follows the square, so it takes the triangle, and the row then starts again with the pentagon.
items.answer: A triangle, and then a pentagon again
items.question: A row goes pentagon, square, triangle, pentagon, square, and then an empty place. Which shape goes there, and which comes after it?
items.checkpoint: A row can lose a side at each step and then start again from its first shape.
items.misconception: Looking for a shape with two sides after the triangle, when a closed shape with straight sides needs at least three.

steps: Child 4 is drawn, so child 4 bats first.
The order then follows the numbers, so after 4 comes 5.
5 is the last number, so the order goes round to 1, then 2, then 3.
items.question: Five children bat in turn in the order 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, going round. Today a draw says child 4 bats first. Write the whole order.
items.checkpoint: After the last number the order goes round to the first, and each child keeps the same neighbour.
items.misconception: Stopping after 5 and leaving out the children whose numbers come before the one drawn.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Star, moon, star, moon, star, and then an empty place. What goes in the empty place?
items.final_answer: Moon, because star and moon take turns

items.question: Square, square, circle, square, square, circle, square, and then an empty place. What goes there, and what is the group that repeats?
items.final_answer: Square, and the group is square, square, circle

items.question: A dot sits at the bottom of a plus shape, then at the left, then at the top. It moves one place round clockwise each time. Where does it sit next?
An arrow points down and makes a quarter turn clockwise at every step. Which way does it point after eight steps?
items.final_answer: Down again, because four quarter turns make a full turn and eight make two full turns

items.question: A row goes triangle, square, pentagon, triangle, square, and then an empty place. What goes in the empty place?
items.final_answer: A pentagon, because the shapes gain one side each time, three, four, five, and then start again at three

items.question: A row starts with a seven-sided shape and loses one side at every step. How many shapes are in the row before it has to start again?
items.final_answer: Five: seven sides, six, five, four and three. A closed shape with straight sides needs at least three, so the row then starts again

items.question: Two teams of five players take turns in the order of their numbers, going round, and one draw sets the start for both teams. The draw is 3. Write each team's order.
items.final_answer: 3, 4, 5, 1, 2 for both teams, because the same draw starts both

items.question: Six players take turns in the order 1 to 6, going round. Player 2 goes last. Who went first?

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: draws a bracket over the cells the child thinks repeat
lights every copy of the bracketed group along the strip
turns an arrow or a dot one quarter turn clockwise at a time
counts the quarter turns made and closes at four
writes how many straight sides each shape has under its cell
lays a numbered order round a circle
picks the number that goes first
sets one draw for two teams at once

teaching_notes: Make one repeating row with real things on a desk before the tool is opened, beads or caps or pencils, and ask for the smallest group that repeats rather than for the next thing. Give a group of three early. Every row of the recap's matching question alternates two shapes, and a child can fill all four blanks by copying the cell two places back without having found anything, so a group of three is the first place the habit is tested. Do the quarter turn with a paper arrow held flat on the desk and turned the way a clock's hands move, and count the turns aloud until four brings it home. The row of shapes that loses a side is worth a question the page does not ask: why does it start again after the triangle? Because a closed shape with straight sides needs at least three. The closing task on the last page is an order that goes round, four performers in the order of their numbers starting from a number drawn by lot. Name nobody; call each performer by their number. Say out loud that one draw sets the start for both teams in an event, because the page implies it and never states it, and a child who draws again for the second team fills a different table.
generation_prompt: Build a picture pattern tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A long horizontal strip of equal cells runs across the working area, each cell holding a shape, an arrow, or a dot on a plus-shaped outline, with the last few cells empty. A bracket control lets the child drag a bracket over any run of cells; the strip then lights every copy of that run along its whole length at once, and any copy that does not match is left unlit so the mismatch can be seen. A turn dial sits under the first empty cell in a row of arrows or dots and turns its arrow one quarter turn clockwise per tap, with a small ring beside it that counts the turns and closes at four. A side counter writes the number of straight sides under each shape in the row. A ring bay at one side lays up to eight numbered places evenly round a circle; a draw control picks the number that goes first, and an order line beside the ring fills as the child reads the order off the ring, with an arc drawn from the last number back to the first. A two rings control sets the same draw for two rings side by side. Shapes are drawn at one size, one to a cell, never overlapping. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Find the shapes that come round again. Put a bracket over them. Turn the arrow the same way each time. Count the sides of each shape. After the last number, go round to the first.
